We spent $2M telling the world to stop hiring humans.\
\
Today we’re taking it back.\
\
And in even more shocking news: Artisan is hiring a human BDR.\
\
The billboards were never a lie. Ava the AI BDR does outreach better than most humans. But she can’t legally cold call. She can’t shake a hand at a conference. She can’t be human.\
\
So we built the tools for the humans. A dialer and a full rep toolkit, inside Artisan. Your reps do the human work. Ava does EVERYTHING else. Leads, signals, personalization, objections, meetings booked, all autonomous.\
\
That’s already how the biggest teams on Artisan run. One of them has Ava working alongside 1,000+ human reps.\
\
Now we’re proving the super-BDR thesis on ourselves. The one BDR we hire will outperform most companies’ entire team. \

Stop hiring humans led to billions of impressions and millions in ARR. But it’s time for the next era.\

Artisan, the AI sales agent startup founded by Jaspar Carmichael-Jack, recently raised $25 million in Series A funding, led by Glade Brook Capital, with participation from Y Combinator, Day One Ventures, HubSpot Ventures, and others. Founded in 2024, Artisan initially garnered attention with its bold “Stop Hiring Humans” campaign, positioning itself in the rapidly growing AI sales development representative (SDR) market. Despite early-stage challenges, including customer churn and issues with AI performance, the company has made significant strides, refining its AI agent, Ava, and achieving $5 million in annual recurring revenue with 250 customers. Artisan is also working on new AI products, such as Aaron for inbound messaging and Aria, a meeting manager assistant, both set to launch by the end of 2025. Carmichael-Jack, who co-founded the company with Sam Stallings, continues to steer Artisan as CEO, emphasizing the importance of human labor in AI-driven environments.\

AI can find the leaks, organize the data, and give you more answers.\

It still can’t make the hard call for you—and that’s usually where clarity breaks down.
Elasticity = cheaper marginal customers
Does your ad spend get you new customers?

A higher CAC doesn’t automatically mean you should stop scaling.\
\
What matters is how much your margins can support, and whether that next dollar of ad spend is building a healthier business or just buying more revenue.\
\
Comment SCALE and I’ll send you the framework.

Doubling revenue shouldn’t mean doubling your problems.\
\
Every hire, inventory order and increase in ad spend is a decision that affects what you keep from that growth.\
\
The bigger the business gets, the more expensive it becomes to make those decisions without a model.

I see this again and again: an e-commerce business is growing, the numbers look good, but there’s never enough cash.\
\
Profit on paper doesn’t mean cash in the bank. Inventory, supplier terms, and your cash conversion cycle all affect what’s actually available.\
\
In this video, I break down what I’d check first and what I’d change.

Luca Pacioli: Ancient Double-Entry Bookkeeping, published by Mercury. @mercuryfi \
\
A contemporary republication of John B. Geijsbeek’s 1914 English translation of Luca Pacioli’s landmark 1494 treatise on bookkeeping. Redesigned and newly typeset at the exact dimensions of the original 1914 edition, the book brings the translation together with original pages, diagrams and historical material in a new editorial structure.\
\
Pacioli’s text was the first printed description of double-entry bookkeeping, codifying the system of debits, credits, journals and ledgers that became foundational to modern accounting. The subject has particular relevance for Mercury, whose financial tools for businesses are built on many of these same underlying principles.\
\
The section-sewn hardcover features an exposed spine, silver foil typography and a violet-painted top edge, and is housed in a flexographically printed box.\
\

\
“After a few years of wondering ‘what if,’ I’m grateful for the opportunity we had to give Dorje a try,” Nick says. “It couldn’t have happened without the hard work and positive energy from the entire team.”\
\
Nick calls Dorje Lhakpa a “diamond in the sky.” The route is extremely steep—ranging from 45 to 50 degrees, with some sections reaching 55 degrees. This climb marks the end of a multi-year quest that started when Nick first saw a photo of Dorje Lhakpa online.\
\
“All it took was that one photo of the South Face and I became obsessed,” Nick says. “It towers into the sky and can be seen from Kathmandu on a clear day. It looks so impossibly big and steep, but at the same time it’s exactly what we look for in the big mountains: a line where imagination meets reality.” \
\
This achievement is not only a major milestone in mountaineering, but also shows how Nick’s curiosity drives him to explore what’s beyond the next ridge.\
\
“We’re incredibly proud of Nick, Billy and Adam,” says Jean-Baptiste Cotte, Patagonia’s Snow category marketer. “Nick has dreamed about this objective for years, and their success is a testament to curiosity, perseverance, and the spirit of exploration. My brutally honest advice to someone who wants to make a lot of money:\

The only way to make a lot of money is to create a lot of value.\
\
No one hands out money. No one is going to pay you just because they like you or think you’re cool.\

Money earned is a direct byproduct of value created.\

\
You create value by doing three things:\
\
- Identify problems\
- Create solutions\
- Scale those solutions\
\
It’s not talking about the thing, it’s not brainstorming about the thing, it’s not asking about the thing, it’s not thinking about the thing. The only way to create value is by doing the thing.\

\
What problems can you solve for the people around you?\
\
Figure them out, solve them, scale that solution.\
\
That’s how you make money.\

1 tsp Sesame oil\
1 tbsp Sesame seeds\
1 tsp soy sauce\
100g Tesco microwavable basmati cooked rice\
2 Tesco Golden Egg Yolks, beaten\
1 handful Tesco grated four cheese\
1 tbsp tinned sweetcorn, drained\
1 spring onion, sliced\
Green salad, to serve\
\
1. Heat the sesame oil and soy sauce in a medium frying pan over a medium heat.\
2. Add the cooked rice and sesame seeds, mixing well to coat. Spread the rice evenly across the pan and toast for 2 minutes.\
3. Pour over the beaten eggs, then sprinkle with the cheese, sweetcorn and spring onion. Cover with a lid and cook for 3–4 minutes, until the eggs are set and the cheese has melted.\

- Why he refused an offer to evacuate Kyiv.\
- The 64km Russian military convoy advancing towards the capital.\

- What he believes it will take to end the war.\

He spoke about meeting parents whose children had been killed. Some, he explained, simply ask him for a hug.\
\
And as he spoke, there were tears in his eyes.\
\
Whatever your views on the war or the decisions made by those involved, this is a rare opportunity to hear his account of events that have changed millions of lives.\
\
Because behind every map, every headline and every political decision, there are real people.\

Business is personal development disguised as business.\
\
You learn what gives you energy.\
What drains you.\
Who you actually want to work with.\
And what kind of life you’re really trying to build.\

I don’t want a business full of:\

“I have to call this person.”\
“I have to take this project.”\
“I have to do this thing I hate.”\
\
Follow the work that feels alive.\
\
Because when the work energizes you, 12 hours can disappear.\
\
When it drains you, everyone feels it.\
\
Including your clients.\
\
What are you still doing in your business that you already know you don’t want to do?

Neediness makes you cheaper.\
\
The moment a client feels how badly you need the job, the power shifts.\
\
You start discounting.\
Explaining.\
Chasing.\
Trying to make the deal happen.\
\
And ironically, that makes them want you less.\
\
The energy is simple:\
I’m good with you.\
I’m good without you.\
\
That doesn’t mean arrogance.\
\
It means believing your value doesn’t disappear because someone says no.\
\
The less desperately you need the deal, the stronger your position becomes.\
\
Can you walk into the room knowing they need to earn access to you too?\

There is a profound vulnerability in being a patient.\
 \
When something feels wrong, when you're scared, when you no longer recognize yourself or understand what's happening in your own body, you're placing enormous trust in another human being.\
 \
As a physician, I never want to lose sight of what that means.\
 \
Patients come to us with more than symptoms. They come with fears, questions, uncertainty, and the hope that someone will help them make sense of what they're experiencing. The doctor-patient relationship is built on trust, not just medical expertise. And that trust is shaped by how we listen, how we respond, and how we care for people when the answers aren't immediately clear.\
 \
We won't always have the answers. But we can always make room for the questions. We can acknowledge uncertainty without dismissing someone's experience. We can remember that what may be a routine appointment for us can be one of the most frightening moments in someone else's life.\
 \
Being listened to isn't a courtesy. It's part of being cared for. And every patient deserves that.\
\
